articles.summary: Democratic California Gov. Gavin Newsom says he will decide on a 2028 presidential bid by early January, but Kamala Harris could complicate those plans.
articles.body: Democratic California Gov. Gavin Newsom said Thursday that he will decide within the next two months whether to seek the presidency, revealing that he plans to make up his mind by early January about a potential 2028 bid. Newsom, who will leave office in January, was asked about his presidential aspirations while attending the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference in Antalya, Turkey. "As it relates to 2028, we'll make that decision in the next few months," Newsom told Turkey's Anadolu news agency. "I'll make the determination at the beginning of the year," he continued. "So we'll spend the next few weeks with the family and make a decision early January." GAVIN NEWSOM SEEKS COUNSEL FROM ‘MASTER’ BILL CLINTON AS HE PLOTS PROJECT 2029 Newsom has long been discussed as a potential 2028 contender, frequently mentioned among possible Democratic candidates, including Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., and Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga. However, fellow Californian and 2024 Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris could complicate Newsom's plans if she decides to launch another White House bid. Newsom previously said he would not run for president if Harris entered the race. "I don't know if she runs, but we'll see," Newsom told CNN's Jake Tapper in a September interview. "But I wouldn't run if she ran." "If she runs, you will not," Tapper responded. NEWSOM ROASTED ONLINE FOR 'STAGED' FLY-FISHING INTERVIEW WITH CNN ANCHOR WHERE HE DROPPED MAJOR 2028 HINT "Of course not. Why would I?" Newsom said. "I wouldn't do that to her ... I wouldn't do that to you. I wouldn't waste everyone's time. Who needs that?" Newsom also suggested during the interview that spectators would feast on the "mutual-assured destruction" among Democrats competing for the nomination. "I mean, you do whatever you want. I don't care," Tapper told Newsom. "But [the] counterargument would be, like, you know, she had her shot. And you've never run, and she's run twice." "Yeah," Newsom responded. "I mean, that'd be the approach to the campaign, certainly. That'd be the case you'd make. Pretty good one, actually. That's objectively true." KATHY HOCHUL ENTERTAINS MASSIVE POLITICAL PROMOTION AS DEMOCRATS LOOK AHEAD TO 2028 Newsom, who is term-limited after 2026, outlined his political timeline just over a week after Republicans suffered sweeping defeats in the midterm elections, losing control of both chambers of Congress and several traditionally Republican strongholds. Newsom said he was "particularly pleased with the outcome of the election." "Donald Trump's presidency, as we know it, ended last week in the U.S.," he said. "It was an historic rebuke of his tenure and now it's incumbent upon those that were successful to govern and to lead my party. The Democratic Party now has to set forth a positive alternative agenda to Donald Trump." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News Digital's Joseph A. Wulfsohn contributed to this report.

articles.title: Ada Colau, a Jordi Wild: "Florentino Pérez tiene 4.900 millones de euros, yo creo que puede pagar 300"
articles.standfirst: La candidata de Frente Amplio pasa por 'The Wild Project'
articles.summary: La candidata de Frente Amplio pasa por 'The Wild Project'
articles.body: Ada Colau, candidata de Frente Amplio, ha pasado por el pódcast 'The Wild Project', de Jordi Wild. La dirigente catalana, exalcaldesa de Barcelona, se ha sometido a una extensa entrevista por parte del youtuber, una iniciativa que ha marcado la agenda política en las últimas semanas. "Junto al PP, sois los dos que me lo habéis puesto más fácil para hacer todo esto. Desde el primer momento. No es fácil venir aquí, podríais haber pasado", ha destacado Jordi Wild. Por su parte, Ada Colau ha explicado por qué ha aceptado la invitación: "La primera razón fue mi hijo. Lo primero que me dijo mi hijo de 15 años es 'tienes que ir con Jordi Wild'. También ha motivos políticos. Llegas especialmente a gente joven y es uno de los temas pendientes de la política". Preguntada por sus declaraciones en las que afirmaba que nunca volvería a la política activa, la exalcadesa de Barcelona ha aclarado su postura. Ada Colau ha recordado que en varias ocasiones le han propuesto volver a la primera línea política. "Me propusieron ser ministra en el gobierno de Sánchez y dije que no y a las europeas y dije que no. Me ha ido bien estar fuera de la política institucional. No soy política profesional. Dije que no volvería a no ser que hubiera una situación en la que pudiera ser especialmente útil y esta lo es", ha afirmado. La exalcaldesa de Barcelona ha comentado que la vida de la gente, pese a la subida "histórica" del SMI, "sigue siendo muy difícil en el día a día". "Lo lógico es hacer una reforma fiscal donde quien más tiene pague más", ha apuntado. Ada Colau ha puesto un ejemplo claro: "Florentino Pérez tiene 4.900 millones de euros. Pues si ahora está pagando sobre sus beneficios 150 millones de euros yo creo que puede pagar 300". "Florentino Pérez debería entender que para que funcione la sanidad pública, la educación pública, las pensiones, para que el país no se rompa...", ha planteado. Jordi Wild ha reconocido que una de las cosas que más le decepcionan de la política es que los dirigentes falten a su palabra. "Entiendo que haya una desconfianza general hacia la política", ha señalado. Ada Colau ha confesado que se planteó dejar la candidatura de Frente Amplio tras la falta de acuerdo con Podemos y ERC: "Claro que se me pasó por la cabeza, lo que quería es que fuera lo más unitaria posible. Estaba dispuesta a todo, a apartarme yo misma. Había otra formación que no quiso ni sentarse a hablar". La exalcadesa de Barcelona ha comentado que no tiene ningún indicio de que Zapatero, expresidente, sea culpable, aunque ha valorado igualmente la situación. "A Zapatero le han encontrado joyas por más de un millón de euros, es posible que sea legal, pero a mí no me gusta y no tengo nadie cercano a mí que tenga joyas de más de un millón de euros", ha reflexionado Ada Colau. "Para cambiar las cosas tienes que entrar. No es que quiera ser su amiga, ni de unos ni de otros. Pero quiero cambiar la realidad. Tienes que entrar a un juego en el que no dominas todas las normas", ha comentado Ada Colau. La exalcaldesa ha valorado el accidente de Renfe en Toledo: "He sido muy crítica con que se insinuara que esto podía ser un fallo humano". Jordi Wild le ha preguntado si el presidente, Pedro Sánchez, debería dimitir. "Para mí lo importante es asumir responsabilidades. Lo primero es que tienes que investigar", ha explicado Ada Colau, que se ha referido a la liberalización del sector ferroviario. Jordi Wild ha insistido: "Tú contratas a una empresa que gestionas y que vigilas. No es por ser malo, a mí me indigna porque yo he usado mucho el tren. La gente tiene pánico de ir en un tren. La verdad es que hay siete años de un gobierno anterior (a los últimos accidentes) que no ha hecho nada para mejorarlo, en todo caso lo ha empeorado. El AVE empezó con que si llegaba cinco minutos tarde te devolvían el dinero. Ya se veía que la cosa que no iba bien y la línea estaba deteriorada". Jordi Wild le ha preguntado a Ada Colau por qué dejó Twitter (ahora X) y por qué ha regresado: "Cuando lo dejé es porque era alcaldesa y tenía muchísimo trabajo que hacer. En ese momento estaba polarizando la política, el algoritmo la premiaba mucho. Me hacía perder tiempo, muchas horas y yo como alcaldesa tenía otras cosas que hacer. Otra gente puede estar en Twitter, a mí no me convenía". Cuando regresó a la política de primera línea, ha comentado Colau, decidió junto a su equipo regresar a la plataforma. "Estábamos en desventaja, tenemos mucho menos dinero que otros partidos para hacer campaña. Yo personalmente, respondiendo a tu pregunta, como Ada Colau, no voy a volver a Twitter. En esta campaña, donde va a ser difícil y no va a haber mucho tiempo, no hay que desaprovechar ningún canal aunque sea hostil", ha reflexionado. Jordi Wild ha insistido en que Ada Colau ha roto una promesa a la ciudadanía al volver a presentarse y la candidata de Frente Amplio ha insistido en que siempre se puede cambiar de opinión si se justifican los motivos. Tras unos segundos de debate, la exalcaldesa de Barcelona ha subrayado la importancia de estos comicios: "No son unas elecciones cualquiera con el desahucio de Maricarmen. Me marcó, como a muchísima gente. Nos partió el alma. Fue el detonante la respuesta masiva de la gente". La exalcaldesa de Barcelona ha apuntado que Elon Musk, propietario de la plataforma, está alineado con la extrema derecha. "Hizo el saludo nazi", ha señalado. "Para hacer política tranquila, Twitter no sería el lugar ideal. Hay que exponerse también ahí", ha comentado. Ada Colau, nacida en Barcelona hace 52 años, es la candidata de Frente Amplio a la presidenta del Gobierno. La exalcaldesa de Barcelona, con pasado como activista, especialmente ligada a la lucha social por el acceso a la vivienda, lleva años desvinculada de la primera línea de la política, pero ahora ha regresado como la apuesta de la formación de izquierdas para sumar el máximo número de escaños posible.

articles.title: Jordi Wild y Ada Colau ponen en duda que la final del Mundial 2030 se celebre en Marruecos: “Infantino se va con el rey de vacaciones”
articles.standfirst: Tema tenso y la visión de Ada Colau
articles.summary: Tema tenso y la visión de Ada Colau
articles.body: El tema del mundial de fútbol y la polémica en torno a Marruecos y España ha ido creciendo de forma exponencial y en este caso Jordi Wild ha querido meter el dedo en la yaga con Ada Colau. Es cuando el youtuber ha entrado de lleno para saber lo que piensa el dirigente catalana. "¿Tienes es misma sensación que hay pleitesía hacia Marruecos?", empezaba diciendo Wild. A lo que Ada Colau: "Derechos humanos por delante de finales de un mundial. Pero la Liga española ha tenido actuaciones más que discutidas. Como Arabia Saudí". Si tuviera mano: "Intenaría que los derechos humanos pasara por delante del bussiness de la FIFA. Nos todos los países son perfectos. Si me lo preguntas, me gustaría revisar que la final se haga en Marruecos si no se dan unas condiciones determinadas" Colau ha tenido que mojarse con la final del Mundial y la correlación de Marruecos con España pero pone un obstáculo al respecto: "Marruecos es superamigo de Trump y de Infantino. Son unas relaciones más fuertes que puedan tener los presidentes de España".. a lo que se añadía: "“Infantino se va con el rey de vacaciones”. Eso sí, la dirigente de Frente Amplio añadía: "Ojalá que la negociaciones del Mundial nos permitiera mejorar la relación con Marruecos".

articles.title: Pence leaves door open to 2028 White House run, issues stark warning to GOP after midterm disaster
articles.summary: Mike Pence says he's heard from people across the country about a 2028 presidential bid and warns the GOP must return to conservative principles.
articles.body: EXCLUSIVE - Former Vice President Mike Pence isn't ruling out another run for the White House in 2028, telling Fox News Digital that he has heard from people across the country about a potential presidential bid. The former vice president also delivered a warning to his party following the GOP's severe setbacks in the 2026 midterm elections, arguing that Republicans risk another defeat unless they abandon departures from the traditional conservative principles that have defined the party for decades. Pence, who unsuccessfully campaigned for the 2024 Republican presidential nomination, said at an event in September at the Economic Club of Washington that he had "no plans" to run for president or any other elected office in 2028. But in his first interview since the midterms, Pence appeared to leave the door open to another White House bid, telling Fox News Digital he's received outreach urging him to consider another White House bid. ONLY ON FOX NEWS: PENCE DELIVERS SCATHING REBUKE TO VANCE, TRUMP "We've been hearing from a lot of people around the country. I've been very humbled by that," he said. Pence didn't reveal any timeline for making a 2028 decision. Instead he repeatedly emphasized that "the most important thing is that we win the presidency in 2028. And to do that, I think it will be essential that we focus first on what we're for before we focus on who we're for." WILL TRUMP AVOID MAKING AN ENDORSEMENT IN THE 2028 GOP NOMINATION RACE? Pence, who has seen Advancing American Freedom, his policy and advocacy organization, dramatically expand over the past year, highlighted that he's going to "continue to lean into advocating that broad mainstream conservative agenda that's defined the Republican Party for the last 50 years." "The truth is if, if we don't return the Republican Party to the principles of a strong defense, limited government, fiscal responsibility, and the right to life, it won't matter who we nominate in 2028." Pence partially blames the GOP's midterm shellacking, which saw the Democrats win a large House majority and also regain control of the Senate, on what he argues is President Donald Trump's second term retreat from conservative principles and towards a populist agenda. Pence, who served as Trump's first term vice president, claimed that "this version of Republicanism was just rejected by the American people" in what he called "the wreckage of the 2026 midterm elections." Asked for comment, White House Spokesman Davis Ingle told Fox News Digital, "Mike Pence’s total and complete lack of courage caused untold damage to our great country. If Republican voters cared what Mike Pence had to say, he wouldn’t have had to drop out of the presidential race months before the Iowa caucuses." VANCE, CRUZ, DESANTIS DIAGNOSE GOP'S MIDTERM DISASTER AS 2028 BATTLE BEGINS Looking ahead, Pence said, " I don't know what the future holds, but all of my energies, all of my focus and my calling now is to be a champion and an advocate for the conservative principles that have defined our party, led us to our greatest successes, and always made America strong and prosperous and free." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Asked if he doesn't run, he could support Vice President JD Vance or Secretary of State Marco Rubio if either seeks the GOP nomination, Pence answered, "What I'm gonna be looking for is men and women who embrace that historic traditional conservative agenda of the Republican Party." He argued that "there's a lot of folks on the populist right that suggest that people that that hew to that old Reagan tradition don't know what time it is, and I think the midterm elections have given a verdict on their approach to Republicanism."

articles.title: Stockpiling for disaster: What does the Pentagon know that it isn’t telling us?
articles.summary: If American civilians are at risk, they have a right to know.
articles.body:
Living off the grid is no picnic. While people may choose to unplug for the weekend and escape the noise of the city, the simple pleasures of a few days outdoors is very different from surviving when there are no utilities or modern amenities available.

That’s why it’s alarming that while the U.K. has instructed its citizens to stockpile food, water and cash for a possible massive disruption, the Pentagon has only advised military bases to plan to operate off the grid for up to 90 days. American civilian leaders have been left out of the loop.

It is no secret that we are in a war with Iran. Iran is not a backwater. It has been a pariah state for decades, but it does have the technical abilities and know-how to launch a cyberattack. Whether there is a specific threat that has raised concerns within the Department of Defense, or Secretary Pete Hegseth has just learned of his adversaries’ capabilities, we don’t know.

Either way, a cyberattack by Iran that could disrupt civilian life in the U.S. and in other Western countries is not outside the realm of possibility.

That’s why the Department of Defense’s handling of the threat is so troubling. If American civilians are at risk, they have a right to know. Just as important for managing the threat, America’s governors and mayors must be read in to the situation to begin planning for the worst.

When I managed the aftermath of Hurricane Katrina , none of that effort was a one-man show. We organized people and resources from across the federal, state and local levels. That’s how we were able to get food, water and medical care to those in need. It’s also how we were able to restore safety and order and begin the long process of rebuilding after a major disaster.

If there is an attack, or if some other tragedy strikes, the situation cannot be handled solely from behind a desk in Washington. State officials and local leaders should be made aware of any threats to their people and be brought into the planning process as much as possible. They will be part of the disaster management and recovery regardless.

Three months without power isn’t a laughing matter. It would mean far worse than the temporary loss of creature comforts. Ninety days without an electrical grid would mean no heating and refrigeration, disruptions to food, water and fuel supplies and more. People, whether sick in the hospital or completely healthy, would die otherwise completely preventable deaths. While a sound plan for civilian leaders may not save every life, it would go far in maintaining stability and stopping countless additional tragedies from ever happening.

If there is an imminent threat, the least the Pentagon can do is read civilian leaders in as soon as possible, so that emergency plans can be updated and resources can be put into position. And if the threat is not imminent, or the concern is more general, then that should also be made clear. No one benefits from panic or confusion.

For those concerned about protecting their households during a disaster, my advice remains consistent. Purchase several days of nonperishable food. Keep multiple gallons of water for each member of the family for every anticipated day of disruption. Stock up on batteries, and make sure you have any and all prescriptions filled. And in case your phone cannot be recharged or cellular service is lost, keep a battery-operated or hand-cranked radio as well, so you can continue to monitor the situation.

With a few simple steps, you can help ensure your family’s safety, even when the lights go out.

Lt. Gen. Russel L. Honoré (Ret.) is the former commander of the U.S. First Army who led recovery efforts after Hurricane Katrina. Following the Jan. 6, 2021 attack on the U.S. Capitol, he led the official review of Capitol security.

articles.title: Senate Republican on Vance blaming midterm GOP losses on Iran war: ‘Put down the crack pipe’
articles.summary: Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) criticized Vice President Vance’s claim that Republicans lost the midterms because of the war in Iran, saying the reason behind the party’s sweeping midterm losses is “a lot deeper than that.” “This loss was not because of Iran. That might have played a part, but I don’t think every statewide Republican…
articles.body:
Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) criticized Vice President Vance’s claim that Republicans lost the midterms because of the war in Iran, saying the reason behind the party’s sweeping midterm losses is “a lot deeper than that.”

“This loss was not because of Iran. That might have played a part, but I don’t think every statewide Republican in Texas lost their election, every single one, because they think American foreign policy is too interventionist,” Kennedy told CNN’s Kasie Hunt on Thursday. “I mean, put down the crack pipe.”

Vance shared his thoughts on GOP midterm losses in a lengthy post to the social platform X after the election, writing, “the reason we lost is the war.”

Kennedy, who said before the election Republicans needed to do more to address high prices and inflation, pointed to economic concerns as a primary reason for his party’s defeat.

“I think the Democrats did a better job, much better job, of acknowledging the economic pain that the American people are going through,” Kennedy said.

“I’ve heard President Trump say before, ‘Well, you know, this inflation started under President Biden,’ and that’s true,” he added. “But the economy belongs to President Trump. He might not have fathered this child, but he’s got to raise it. And people are hurting.”

Both the Iran war and the economy were weak points for Trump in approval polls, but inflation and the cost of living were consistently his worst issue — despite it being a key campaign message of his in 2024.

An Economist/YouGov poll conducted after the election found that 67 percent of Americans disapproved of the president’s handling of the economy, slightly worse than the 61 percent who disapproved of his foreign policy.

The issues were intertwined at times, as the war skyrocketed gas and diesel prices , which have remained elevated for much of the year. The president also said the war would be over in only a few weeks, but there is still no resolution to the conflict that began in late February.

Those issues contributed to a brutal midterm environment for the GOP, in which Democrats picked up more than 40 House seats and at least eight Senate seats, with one race outstanding.

Now, with the election over, members of both parties are already looking ahead to 2028. Vance is considered a top presidential candidate for Republicans, but Kennedy said he did not think the vice president “did himself any favors” with his postelection analysis. The Louisiana Republican did not rule out seeking the presidency but said he plans to run for reelection.

“I don’t know, Kasie. I mean, I’m planning on running for reelection to the Senate, but things are getting weirder and weirder and weirder around here,” Kennedy said.

articles.title: The midterm avalanche reveals a new political geography
articles.summary: It’s probably time to toss those red-blue election maps we’ve become so used to since 2000.
articles.body:
Nobody predicted the stunning sweep and depth of Democratic gains in last week’s midterm elections. More than a wave, it was an avalanche that revealed new contours in America’s political geography.

It’s probably time to toss those red-blue election maps we’ve become so used to since 2000. They show the main parties hunkered down behind static battle lines, with serious electoral competition confined to a dwindling number of swing states and districts.

The post-midterm map looks strikingly different. In addition to giving Democrats imposing majorities in Congress, U.S. voters in nearly every county in the country shifted in a blue direction. They won federal and state races across the upper and deep South and the broad middle from Ohio to Iowa and Kansas , enlarging the political battlefield and potentially adding a slew of new swing states.

Democrats scored big down ballot gains . They’re poised to control 30 governor’s mansions, up from 24, and have 22 trifecta wins — governors plus both legislative houses — to the Republicans’ 18.

What happened in Texas was jaw-dropping. Democratic State Rep. James Talarico trounced Republican Ken Paxton by 12 points in a state Trump carried by nearly 14 points . Gina Hinojosa ousted Gov. Greg Abbott (R), another MAGA favorite, to become Texas’s first Democratic governor since 1995 and its first Latina governor ever. Democrats also flipped the Texas House for the first time since 2003.

With 40 Electoral College votes , Texas was the grandest midterm prize of all. It’s been the mainstay of Republican strength in the Trump era, and if it truly becomes competitive in presidential years, the Republicans’ path to power could narrow to a rocky goal trail.

Also smothered in the blue avalanche were Republican efforts to protect their seats by redrawing district boundaries before the next census. Their gerrymandering backfired, galvanizing Black voters in the South and yielding just two seats . Democrats claimed six seats .

Euphoric Democrats need to keep reminding themselves that the midterm vote was a harsh reprimand of Trump, not a vote of confidence in them. Many of his 2024 voters saw his inflationary tariffs and attack on Iran as breaking his campaign promises to drive the cost of living down and avoid embroiling the nation in “ endless wars .”

Republicans got walloped as lots of those disillusioned voters stayed home and groups that moved toward him four years ago — Hispanics, young voters, independents and moderates — swung back to Democrats.

“The president’s coalition is shattered and depressed, with every faction blaming the other, leading to a generational wipeout,” says conservative political analyst Sean Trende.

Compared to 2024, Democrats saw net gains of 30 points among Hispanics, 34 points among young voters and 20 points among independents in House races. Most encouraging of all, Democrats at least temporarily stopped the defection of working class, non-college voters from their coalition. White non-college voters moved 14 points towards Democrats.

These voters historically had backed Democrats at a higher rate than voters with college degrees until 2012. After Barack Obama won them by four points in his 2012 reelection, working class voters backed the insurgent Trump by six points in 2016. In 2024, he won them by 13 points, the biggest winning margin for a Republican presidential candidate since Ronald Reagan.

Trump’s ability to bond with non-college voters seemed to cement the political realignment that’s reshaped both major parties in this century. It’s based on educational polarization. In recent elections, Democrats have gained ground mainly with college grads and urban professionals, while Trump kicked traditional conservatives to the curb and turned Republicans into a populist blue-collar party.

Trading social bases has been a disaster for Democrats. First off, non-college voters far outnumber degree holders in the electorate ( 59-41 in the last presidential election ). And the ascendance of college grads in the party has opened a cultural rift between educated elites and ordinary Americans who, in Bill Clinton’s words , “work hard and play by the rules.”

Democrats lurched left after 2000 as millennials came of political age. U.S. voters, however, didn’t move with them. According to Gallup , by 2024 55 percent of Democrats identified as liberal, 34 percent as moderate and 9 percent as conservative. In last week’s Fox News exit poll , 26 percent of U.S. voters identified as liberal, 41 percent as moderate and 33 percent as conservative.

Democrats can’t build stable majorities on a base of white college liberals. But the midterm results show that, with the right kind of candidates — focused on pocketbook concerns, pragmatic rather than dogmatic, culturally mainstream — they can win anywhere in the country.

Democrats should seize the opportunity now to build a new center-left majority that strikes a better balance between the aspirations and interests of voters on both sides of America’s diploma divide.

Last week’s vote cracked open the door to a new political alignment in the post-Trump era. It can’t get here soon enough.

Will Marshall is founder and president of Progressive Policy Institute.

articles.title: Talarico wants to make Trump’s last 2 years ‘the most productive of any presidency’
articles.summary: Sen.-elect James Talarico (D-Texas) told a gathering of Democrats that they must work with President Trump and cannot wait until a new president takes the oath to start delivering for Americans. Talarico, speaking Thursday to the What’s Next conference in Denver, said Democrats need to work with Trump to deliver on economic relief, political reform…
articles.body:
Sen.-elect James Talarico (D-Texas) told a gathering of Democrats that they must work with President Trump and cannot wait until a new president takes the oath to start delivering for Americans.

Talarico, speaking Thursday to the What’s Next conference in Denver, said Democrats need to work with Trump to deliver on economic relief, political reform and immigration policy in the final two years of his presidency. Talarico will be the first Democratic senator from the Lone Star State since 1988 and regularly advocates for bipartisanship.

“Some of these reforms might not pass until 2029, but the American people cannot wait two years for change. So we must work with President Trump,” Talarico said.

“If President Trump wants the same plaques and portraits and busts as LBJ, we can help make that a reality,” he added, referencing former Texas Sen. and President Lyndon B. Johnson.

The newest Texas senator isn’t the only first-term Democrat to suggest collaboration with the president. Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.) posted to the social platform X on Thursday with mock-ups of “Trump Care” health insurance cards, pushing the president to support universal healthcare.

“Donald, this is on the table. Guarantee healthcare for every American, from cradle to grave,” El-Sayed wrote.

Talarico told the Denver conference that Democrats on Capitol Hill should make the final two years of Trump’s presidency “the most productive of any presidency” in history. He said the current moment is bigger than red versus blue.

“It’s so much bigger than a party. We are tired of being pitted against each other. We’re tired of being told to hate each other. It’s been 10 years of this kind of politics,” Talarico said.

articles.title: White House sends CFTC, SEC nominations to Senate
articles.summary: President Trump on Thursday nominated two officials each to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) and the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). Trump nominated Democrat Kristin Johnson and Republican Steven Levine to the SEC, with their respective terms set to expire in 2029 and 2030. Johnson previously served as a commissioner at the CFTC, after…
articles.body:
President Trump on Thursday nominated two officials each to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) and the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC).

Trump nominated Democrat Kristin Johnson and Republican Steven Levine to the SEC, with their respective terms set to expire in 2029 and 2030.

Johnson previously served as a commissioner at the CFTC, after former President Biden appointed her to the role in 2022.

The president also nominated Democrat Matthew Rowland and Republican Nathan Anonick to the CFTC. Their terms will end in 2028 and 2031, respectively, the White House noted.

All four nominations are subject to Senate approval. The Senate Banking Committee will decide whether to approve the SEC nominees, while the Senate Agriculture Committee has jurisdiction over the CFTC nominees.

Michael Selig, the chair of the CFTC, said the president “made two strong bipartisan picks” in Rowland and Anonik.

“I congratulate them on their nominations and look forward to working with each of them upon their confirmation by the US Senate,” Selig wrote Thursday on social platform X.

Trump’s nominations of Johnson and Rowland mark his first Democratic picks for the CFTC and SEC, which are typically led by five-member bipartisan panels.

Selig is the sole commissioner of the CFTC, while Chair Paul Atkins and Commissioner Mark Uyeda, both Republicans, are the only appointees at the SEC .

Senate Democrats raised concerns about Trump’s lack of Democratic nominations to the two commissions during negotiations over the failed Clarity Act, which aimed to provide a regulatory framework for the digital assets industry.

Democrats in the upper chamber blocked the bill in September, arguing it failed to establish a check on the Trump family’s cryptocurrency ventures.

articles.title: We vote because they can’t: What Democrats must do now to fix mmigration
articles.summary: As Democrats revel in the aftermath of the blue tsunami, they must not take their attention away from the work that immigrant communities elected them to do. “We vote because they can’t” is a promise that must be extended beyond Election Day.
articles.body:
In Texas, voters placed “I Voted” stickers at Lorenzo Salgado Araujo’s memorial, honoring a man whose life was taken by the very government he had no vote to choose. The act captured the spirit of a movement that has taken hold in Latino communities across the country: We vote because they can’t.

For immigrant and mixed-status communities, this month’s Democratic victories represent something much bigger than party politics. They represent the possibility of accountability, a restoration of constitutional protection, and perhaps a shift in how this country treats the people who have long lived in its shadows.

As an immigration attorney who served inside the enforcement system under three presidential administrations, and now represents the people facing it, I keep being asked one question: what changes now?

The path ahead may be difficult, but the work necessary is clear. Restoring constitutional protections for noncitizens requires meaningful limits on immigration enforcement. That begins with confronting what have become known as “Kavanaugh stops,” following Justice Brett Kavanaugh’s concurrence in Noem v. Vasquez Perdomo , which opened the door to immigration stops based on a combination of factors, including perceived ethnicity, language, occupation and location.

Democrats have demanded accountability following the deaths of Alex Pretti and Renee Good and the shooting of Marimar Martinez by immigration officials. With majority control , they will have the oversight powers and authority over funding to turn those demands into action: insisting on independent investigations into excessive force, unlawful arrests and constitutional rights violations, and pressing for referrals to prosecutors where the evidence warrants criminal charges.

Sustained scrutiny is essential to changing an enforcement culture within a Department of Homeland Security that has operated with little meaningful restraint since January 2025.

But perhaps the biggest change in immigration enforcement won’t come from the federal government — it will come from state and local officials. Gina Hinojosa’s election as Texas’s first Latina governor carries particular weight in a state that has become a battleground over immigration. While she cannot rewrite federal immigration law, she can influence how Texas helps enforce it.

One program to watch closely is Section 287(g) of the Immigration and Nationality Act, which allows Immigration and Customs Enforcement to authorize state and local officers to perform certain federal immigration enforcement functions.

These partnerships have expanded dramatically as the administration pushes to increase immigration arrests, with a publicly stated goal of 3,000 a day . They extend immigration enforcement into everyday policing, turning traffic stops for minor violations into potential pathways to detention and deportation. For many noncitizens, a trip to buy coffee can end in family separation through ICE detention and deportation.

Hinojosa voted against Senate Bill 8 in June 2025 as a Texas lawmaker, opposing a mandate requiring Texas sheriffs whose counties operate or contract for a jail to enter immigration enforcement agreements with ICE. But undoing that expansion will require more than an executive order. State law, existing agreements and sheriffs’ independent authority limit what she can accomplish alone.

Those limits do not make her powerless. Hinojosa has argued that border security does not require targeting longtime members of our communities. She can put that distinction into practice by pressing lawmakers to repeal mandatory 287(g) participation, scrutinizing state spending, and challenging the use of Texas resources in abusive enforcement operations. The question now is how far she will go — and whether the legislature will follow.

The road ahead will not be easy. President Trump could veto federal immigration reform legislation. His administration could further delay the adjudication of affirmative immigration petitions, including marriage-based petitions that allow families to remain together. His enforcement policies could continue to face little restraint.

And we may not see fewer people funneled into immigration court just yet. But with sustained pressure, we could begin to see fewer people detained, fewer deaths and more humane conditions for those who remain in custody. A secure border does not require abandoning due process or accepting cruelty as the cost of enforcement.

As Democrats revel in the aftermath of the blue tsunami , they must not take their attention away from the work that immigrant communities elected them to do. “We vote because they can’t” is a promise that must be extended beyond Election Day.

Veronica Cardenas is a former assistant chief counsel for ICE turned immigration attorney and founder of Humanigration .

articles.title: Colom: ‘Not accurate’ to say Schumer recruited him
articles.summary: Sen.-elect Scott Colom (D-Miss.) pushed back on the idea that Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) personally recruited him to run for Senate, saying the people of Mississippi deserve the credit for his upset victory. “He did initially understand that our party has to look south for future leadership,” Colom told MS NOW’s Symone Sanders…
articles.body:
Sen.-elect Scott Colom (D-Miss.) pushed back on the idea that Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) personally recruited him to run for Senate, saying the people of Mississippi deserve the credit for his upset victory .

“He did initially understand that our party has to look south for future leadership,” Colom told MS NOW’s Symone Sanders Townsend in an interview that aired Thursday. “I think that it’s not accurate to say he recruited me, though.”

“I push back on the idea that I was recruited, not as a disrespect to anybody, but just as an acknowledgement that the people of Mississippi are the folks that deserve the credit,” he added.

The Senate Democratic leader was part of a strong performance in the midterm elections. Democrats not only won back the chamber but did so with seats to spare.

Schumer recounted in an interview with The New York Times how he recruited Democratic candidates across the battleground races to ensure his party would be best positioned to reclaim the upper chamber. In the story, the Times said Schumer recruited Colom.

But Schumer now faces a challenge from inside his caucus for his position as Democratic leader, with Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) announcing Thursday evening he would seek the role.

Though the interview was conducted before Van Hollen announced his challenge, Colom did not commit to supporting Schumer, saying, “I got to know my options.”

“I’m looking for a person that’s going to be committed to Mississippi and rural voices,” Colom told Sanders Townsend. “If you’re able to listen to those voices and make sure that you understand their needs and putting them in position to be successful, then that’s the type of leadership I want.”

Colom beat Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R-Miss.) in an upset victory that took more than a week after the election to call. Mississippi is a deep-red state that President Trump won by nearly 23 points in 2024, and voters there have not elected a Democrat for U.S. Senate since 1982.

The senator-elect and the incumbent have history: Former President Biden nominated Colom to be a federal judge, but Hyde-Smith used her ability as his home-state senator to block him from receiving a confirmation hearing. Years later, Colom has defeated Hyde-Smith but said that past experience was not a factor in deciding to challenge her for U.S. Senate.

“I’m a Christian. I mean, I forgive her,” Colom said. “It’s not good for the soul to hold, you know, anger and feelings like that toward somebody.”

Colom said he spoke to Sen. Roger Wicker (R-Miss.), who will soon be his partner in the Senate, and that the two pledged to work together and disagree respectfully.

“He said, ‘If we disagree, we’re going to be respectful about it.’ And you know, we may not agree on everything, but when we disagree, we’ll be respectful,” Colom said. “We’re not a state that can get too bogged down in partisan food fights. We have to be a state that’s focused on delivering for Mississippi.”

articles.title: Garcia: Blanche ‘hasn’t even read the Constitution’
articles.summary: Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.) on Thursday accused Attorney General Todd Blanche of failing to understand the constitutional power of Congress to provide oversight of the executive and judicial branches of government. Blanche has defended recent letters sent by the White House warning Democrats that their planned investigations into the Trump administration could “cross the line”…
articles.body:
Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.) on Thursday accused Attorney General Todd Blanche of failing to understand the constitutional power of Congress to provide oversight of the executive and judicial branches of government.

Blanche has defended recent letters sent by the White House warning Democrats that their planned investigations into the Trump administration could “cross the line” into criminal action.

“Donald Trump is clearly hiding something,” Garcia told MS NOW’s Chris Hayes. “To send out this letter to threaten us, to Todd Blanche to back that up, our job is oversight. I mean, it’s literally in the Constitution.

“The attorney general hasn’t even read the Constitution, apparently, because he doesn’t understand that our job is to actually be a check and balance,” he added.

In an interview with Fox News this week, Blanche said the Department of Justice (DOJ) would “not allow the rhetoric to turn from just honest debate to actual criminal conduct.”

“All they’re talking about is impeachment and investigations and going after companies that want to build jobs in this country,” the attorney general continued. “And that’s unfortunate.”

Garcia, who is poised to head the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee when Democrats take control of the chamber next year , told Trump officials to “ lawyer up ” after his party won control of Congress in the midterm elections.

The California Democrat outlined his top priorities for the oversight panel in the interview with MS NOW, including investigating alleged corruption within President Trump’s family, the mass federal deportation operations, corporate fraud and the DOJ’s investigation into convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

The lawmaker noted he expects the Trump administration to “do everything they can to delay” the probes.

“We’re going to use our legal authority in the Congress to do everything we can to push and actually get our subpoenas in place, our legal requests,” Garcia said.

“But we also understand that we’re working with a DOJ that’s really not interested in following the law, that’s not interested in responding to the Congress, and so we’re going to have to also engage the courts in a way that’s more aggressive than in the past,” he added.

The Hill has reached out to the DOJ for comment.

articles.title: Russia’s economy is reeling — Trump should be raising the pressure if he wants peace
articles.summary: The Graham sanctions law, if allowed to take full effect, could force Putin into earnest negotiations.
articles.body:
The Russian economy appears to be going from bad to worse.

Earlier this week, Elvira Nabuillina, chair of the Russian Central Bank, reported to Russia’s legislature that the bank will not lower its key interest rate, currently standing at 14 percent, due to the potential “harm to the economy” from the inflationary impact.

She acknowledged that “attacks on our oil refineries, other industrial facilities, data centers and logistics hubs have constrained production capacity … excessive growth in demand under current circumstances could accelerate inflation.”

Nabuillina added that “of all possible taxes, a sharp rise in prices is an unfair one,” and “current price pressures remain elevated.” Most notably, gas prices are up 21 percent, and diesel prices by 13.4 percent since the beginning of 2026.

The central bank has increased its forecast for inflation in 2026 from less than 7 percent to 7.6 percent and expects that in 2027 inflation will be reduced to four percent. Those numbers do not seem realistic, and are probably artificially low, however, given the ongoing conflict and Ukrainian attacks on Russian infrastructure.

The high interest rates, even at the levels that the bank has acknowledged, have stunted Russian economic growth, projected at only 0.6 percent for this year. The budget deficit has doubled from 1.6 percent of GDP last year to 3.2 percent in 2026, while government spending is expected to increase by 13 percent due to the cost of the ongoing war with Ukraine.

Meanwhile, Russian forces are stalemated as the war drags on and Ukraine continues to make modest gains on the ground. According to the Institute for the Study of War , “Russian forces have lost the initiative and their offensive capabilities in much of the theater.” The Institute reports that Ukraine regained approximately a net 27 square kilometers in October. More importantly, Russia continues to amass heavy losses. In October, Russian forces lost 54,000 killed or seriously wounded — the highest monthly casualty rate since the invasion began. Ukrainian gains may also be threatening Russian supply lines .

The Russian economy has suffered not only from Ukrainian attacks on oil and gas infrastructure, but also from ongoing sanctions that the U.S., Britain and the European Union have imposed on the Kremlin. Congress further toughened those sanctions when it passed the Lindsay O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act , which President Trump signed on Sept. 18.

The law provides for a 500 per cent tariff on all imported Russian goods, with duties of up to 100 percent on goods from any of the top five importers of Russian oil or gas, as well as on the top five states that facilitate Russian evasion of those sanctions. China and India are among these states.

The Graham law also includes sanctions against Russian President Vladimir Putin, senior military officials and Russian financial institutions and it applied similar new sanctions on Iran.

On Oct. 16, however, having previously agreed to let Russia export diesel fuel, Trump used his authority under the new law to waive most of its sanctions as they affected Russia. Importantly, he did not waive any previously approved sanctions, and the administration still characterizes the war as “Russian aggression.”

The waiver certainly strengthened Putin’s determination to persist with his disastrous invasion and his maximalist demands. Consequently, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky will surely continue to maintain his own demands for a full Russian withdrawal from all occupied Ukrainian oblasts. For Zelensky, and for the country he leads, it is not a matter of history but rather of survival.

The sanctions that the Graham law initially imposed would exacerbate Russia’s straightened economic conditions. They will not force Putin to halt the invasion, but they might force him into more earnest negotiations and a willingness to show some real flexibility for a change.

Indeed, additional sanctions would give Trump’s designated negotiators, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner — who made little progress in their talks in their talks in Abu Dhabi this week — a greater advantage vis-a-vis not only Putin, but also Zelensky. If Putin were to show flexibility suddenly, the Ukrainian president would have little option but to match it.

Were Trump to reconsider his decision and terminate the waiver of sanctions, Putin might realize that Washington is serious about his coming to the negotiating table with some degree of flexibility. As a student of Russian history, he knows that the tsars lost many of the wars they fought.

Dov S. Zakheim is a senior adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies and vice chairman of the board for the Foreign Policy Research Institute. He was undersecretary of Defense (comptroller) and chief financial officer for the Department of Defense from 2001 to 2004 and a deputy undersecretary of Defense from 1985 to 1987.

articles.title: Peltola extends lead after new Alaska Senate ballots count
articles.summary: In the last uncalled Senate race of 2026, former Rep. Mary Peltola (D-Alaska) gained an additional 5,000 newly counted votes Thursday and extended her lead over Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska). Peltola leads Sullivan by 5,800 votes as of 9:30 a.m. EST Friday and surpassed Sullivan in the Alaska Beacon’s calculation of how the vote will…
articles.body:
In the last uncalled Senate race of 2026, former Rep. Mary Peltola (D-Alaska) gained an additional 5,000 newly counted votes Thursday and extended her lead over Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska).

Peltola leads Sullivan by 5,800 votes as of 9:30 a.m. EST Friday and surpassed Sullivan in the Alaska Beacon’s calculation of how the vote will stand after the ranked choice votes are redistributed. If no candidate surpasses 50 percent of the vote, as is the current case, the race will be decided by ranked choice tabulation on Nov. 18.

With more than 83 percent of the anticipated vote counted, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), Peltola has maintained the lead she has had since Election Day even as the sprawling arctic state continues to count votes. She effectively declared victory following Thursday’s ballot drop.

“As more ballots get counted, it is clear Mary’s victory is all but guaranteed and Alaskans have resoundingly rejected Dan Sullivan’s D.C. self dealing,” the Peltola campaign posted to the social media platform X.

DDHQ has yet to call the race. Nevertheless, Peltola claimed she won Thursday’s tabulated ballots by a 2-to-1 margin and that Sullivan is underperforming in traditionally conservative areas.

“When every vote is counted, Mary Peltola will be Alaska’s next United States Senator,” her campaign wrote in the post.

The Alaska Senate race turned into a national controversy after The New York Times revealed that Democrats were behind the campaign of Dan. J Sullivan Jr., a different candidate with the same name as the incumbent.

The Trump administration sued, attempting to block certification of the race if Peltola won by less than the amount of votes cast for the nonincumbent Sullivan. That lawsuit was eventually dismissed .

“Alaskans are ready for a Senator who fights to lower costs and take on DC corruption, and when every vote is counted, Mary will deliver for Alaska,” Peltola’s campaign posted to X.

Peltola surpassed the combined vote tally of both Sullivans earlier this week but has since dipped back below the combined vote count. President Trump has suggested all of Sullivan Jr.’s votes should be awarded to the incumbent Sullivan, claiming there is no other “fair solution.”

articles.title: Trump approval hits record second-term low: Survey
articles.summary: President Trump’s job approval rating sits at a second-term low in a new postelection survey, showing little sign of improvement after his party suffered widespread losses in the midterms. In the new Economist/YouGov poll, 63 percent of Americans said they disapproved of Trump’s job performance, including 52 percent who disapproved strongly, with just 32 percent…
articles.body:
President Trump’s job approval rating sits at a second-term low in a new postelection survey, showing little sign of improvement after his party suffered widespread losses in the midterms.

In the new Economist/YouGov poll , 63 percent of Americans said they disapproved of Trump’s job performance, including 52 percent who disapproved strongly, with just 32 percent approving.

On the issues, foreign policy and the economy remain the president’s weak points. Sixty-one percent of respondents disapproved of Trump’s foreign policy and 67 percent disapproved of his handling of the economy, his worst issue surveyed.

Multiple figures in the Republican Party, including Vice President Vance, were quick to blame the Iran war for GOP losses last week. In the poll, 63 percent of respondents said they wanted the war to end immediately, something Democrats and even some Republicans campaigned on. The war has sent the prices of gas and diesel fuel skyrocketing, contributing to stubborn inflation.

The elevated prices have also made Americans increasingly pessimistic about the economy and its future.

In the poll, a majority of respondents — 55 percent — said the economy is getting worse, while only 13 percent said it was getting better. Seventy-four percent rated the economy either fair or poor.

Majorities in the survey said the cost of gas, food and housing have all gone up a lot. Zero percent of respondents said the cost of gas and food have gone down, after the president promised in his 2024 campaign to bring prices down immediately.

Voters gave Trump poor marks on other issues, too, including his pushes to remake Washington with new and renovated monuments. Fifty percent of respondents said Congress should not allow construction of the White House ballroom to continue, and 57 percent opposed the president’s proposed triumphal arch near Arlington National Cemetery.

And as corruption became a top issue for voters in the final stretch of the campaign, 60 percent of respondents in the Economist/YouGov survey said they think Trump is using his office for personal gain. A combined 82 percent said they believe most or many of the people running the government are corrupt.

With the midterms in the rearview mirror, both parties are beginning to look ahead to 2028 and identify potential White House candidates.

On the Republican side, Vance, with 40 percent support, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, with 33 percent support, lead the pack.

The Democrats’ field appears to be wide open. Former Vice President Kamala Harris leads with 20 percent support, just ahead of Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.), who has 15 percent. Ossoff won reelection last week by nearly 20 points, a notably large margin in battleground Georgia.

The Economist/YouGov survey was conducted among 1,685 U.S. citizens from Nov. 9 to 11. Its margin of error is 3 points.

articles.title: The midterms and a tale of two Americas: Caviar versus cost of living
articles.summary: Journalist Bernard Goldberg criticized President Donald Trump’s perceived detachment from the economic struggles of Americans following a lavish, jungle-themed gala held at Mar-a-Lago shortly before the election.
articles.body:
When President Trump’s critics took to the streets or took seats in front of cable news cameras to tell us that he was behaving more like a mad king than a sane president, it never made sense to me.

I mean, what malevolent king would allow his detractors, the very people who despise him, to take their placards onto the streets to mock and demean him, with cameras rolling for the whole world to see?

Evil kings just don’t tolerate that kind of stuff.

Still, he does remind me of royalty. As I wrote in this space a year ago, almost to the day, Trump reminds me not of a king, but of a queen — Marie Antoinette, who either did or didn’t actually say, “Let them eat cake” while the peasants in France were starving.

Whether she said it matters less to the analogy than what the words have come to represent: a ruler so insulated from ordinary people that their troubles barely register.

On Halloween night, three days before the election, Trump threw a big, glitzy, jungle-themed party at his own Versailles, his palace at Mar-a-Lago in Florida. While Americans were struggling to pay for groceries, the swells at Trump’s gala, decked out in tuxedos and gowns, were sidling up to a bar, to feast on … caviar.

Yahoo News called it “ a camp, spandex-and-glitter-filled affair .” The Washington Post pool report said that people were dressed as leopards and snakes and in “tiger-print dinner jackets.” Peggy Noonan, in the Wall Street Journal, put it this way : “The most clueless 1980s Kennebunkport Republican grandee would never flaunt wealth as these people do in their vulgarity and conceit. In my lifetime the GOP has been many things good and bad, but it had never been decadent.”

Apparently, nobody came dressed as somebody worried about next month’s bills.

Since he launched his war against Iran, Americans practically have had to rob a bank to fill up their cars and trucks at the gas station. And Trump? He’s busy bragging about the gold-laced ballroom he’s building — or his beautiful Reflecting Pool or the giant triumphal arch he’s been envisioning.

Nobody elected Donald Trump because they thought he lived like the rest of us. His name is on buildings. He likes gold. Subtlety has never been his strong suit.

But there’s a difference between voters knowing you’re rich and voters wondering whether you have any idea what they’re going through. Especially when you’ve asked them to believe that you’re the one person who can make their lives better.

While his patrician friends were having a grand old time at Mar-a-Lago, the folks who never get invited to those bashes were struggling to pay their rent or their mortgage or their healthcare and utility bills.

Inside, they were having fun. Outside, a lot of Americans were having anxiety.

And a president who made his political reputation claiming to speak for the forgotten men and women of America seemed awfully preoccupied with people who don’t have to check the price of anything.

Things didn’t end well for Marie Antoinette. She had lost touch with the people outside her palace. And on Election Day, it became clear that Donald Trump had lost touch with millions of Americans outside his palace.

When Americans feel financially insecure, they take it out on the people they hold responsible — this time it was Trump, who called affordability “a hoax” — and his party.

That doesn’t mean everyone who voted Republicans out of office was enthusiastic about the Democrats. Sometimes an election is less an endorsement of the people coming in than a message to the people already there.

And this message wasn’t hard to understand: We’re struggling. You’re celebrating. Something is wrong with this picture.

Of course, unlike the French queen, Trump isn’t facing the guillotine. He’s only facing the prospect of impeachment orchestrated by a Democratic Party that will make his life miserable for the next two years.

If people are having a difficult time paying their bills while Trump and his pals are shoving caviar down their throats at a Mar-a-Lago soiree, things will not end well. If Donald Trump felt the pain of Americans just trying to get by, he had an odd way of showing it.

No, Trump didn’t lose his head as Marie Antoinette did. He only lost the House, the Senate, and a whole lot of power.

But there is some good news for Trump and his courtiers. There will be plenty of cake at the next big, beautiful bash at Mar-a-Lago.

Bernard Goldberg is an Emmy and an Alfred I. duPont-Columbia University award-winning writer and journalist. He is the author of five books and publishes exclusive weekly columns, audio commentaries and Q&As on his Substack page .

articles.title: DOJ instructs its agencies to ‘prioritize’ English over all other languages
articles.summary: The Department of Justice (DOJ) on Friday published a memo designating English as the official language of the agency. “Though not officially designated in the past, English has been our common language since before this Nation’s founding,” the Justice Department wrote in the document posted to the Federal Register, offering public comment over the next…
articles.body:
The Department of Justice (DOJ) on Friday published a memo designating English as the official language of the agency.

“Though not officially designated in the past, English has been our common language since before this Nation’s founding,” the Justice Department wrote in the document posted to the Federal Register , offering public comment over the next 60 days.

“Consequently, agencies should prioritize the English language over all other languages.”

The memo comes in response to an executive order from President Trump signed in March 2025 seeking to designate English as the official language of the United States.

The Justice Department already conducts most of its official business in English and has across administrations run by Democratic and Republican presidents, without a nudge from an executive order.

But the memo argued that agencies should not provide multilingual assistance unless it was required to do so or necessary.

“Moving forward, agencies should promptly identify and review all multilingual assistance programs. Agencies should then determine whether multilingual assistance is required by law or necessary to accomplish an agency’s mission,” the DOJ wrote in the memo.

“If multilingual assistance is neither legally required nor necessary to accomplish the agency’s mission, then the agency should eliminate assistance in favor of English-only operations.”

The Justice Department, through its Civil Rights Division, plays a role in ensuring that multilingual assistance is available as part of the voting process.

The DOJ’s website points to Section 203 of the Voting Rights Act and its obligation to hold election administrators to account for meeting language requirements.

“The United States is a diverse land with a government selected by the votes of its citizens,” the site states.

“Federal law recognizes that many Americans rely heavily on languages other than English, and that they require information in minority languages in order to be informed voters and participate effectively in our representative democracy.”

articles.title: White House staff to need prior approval to meet with lobbyists, under Stephen Miller memo
articles.summary: A new memo from White House chief of staff Stephen Miller says White House staffers need prior approval from the Office of White House Counsel if they want to meet with a lobbyist, a significant shift after the midterm shellacking of the GOP. “No President in history has fought more relentlessly, selflessly or courageously for…
articles.body:
A new memo from White House chief of staff Stephen Miller says White House staffers need prior approval from the Office of White House Counsel if they want to meet with a lobbyist, a significant shift after the midterm shellacking of the GOP.

“No President in history has fought more relentlessly, selflessly or courageously for the American People than President Trump. Following his example, White House staff are expected to dedicate their time unwaveringly to the working people of the nation,” the memo states.

The memo says the prior approval covers meetings on the White House complex with registered lobbyists related to government policy.

A White House official said the memo was sent out last night and is a “much stricter process than before.”

It also says the Office of Public Liaison will continue to serve as the primary point of contact for engagement with external stakeholders.

Republicans lost the House and Senate majorities in last week’s elections, with Democrats winning Senate seats in such previously red states as Texas, South Carolina, Kansas and Mississippi.

While the elections were focused on the economy, affordability and the Iran war, corruption was an underlying theme of the campaigns.

Trump named Miller as his chief of staff on the Friday after the elections. Miller replaced Susie Wiles, who had come under criticism from some administration officials over her ties to lobbying groups.

Former senior health adviser Calley Means criticized Wiles as a career lobbyist concerned only with catering to corporate interests. He claimed Wiles and her former deputy chief of staff James Blair stunted the “Make America Healthy Again” (MAHA) agenda by siding with corporate donors ahead of the midterm elections.

“Just as a statement of economic facts; Susie Wiles, her career has been taking money from the industries and foreign governments who would pay her the most money. That’s what she did. Nobody disputes that,” Means said while on the “ Joe Rogan Experience ” podcast last week.

Means resigned last month from the Department of Health and Human Services over frustrations with the lack of MAHA advancements.

The White House has pushed back on the allegations, saying the administration “has never allowed and will never allow outside groups to influence policy decisions.”

“President Trump is busy executing on his America First agenda that includes the largest working-class tax cuts in history, over a million private sector jobs added to the economy, a sealed shut border, and lowest violent crime to the lowest level in nearly a century,” White House spokesperson Allison Schuster said in a statement.

articles.title: Democrats won, now we need to deliver
articles.summary: Democratic strategist Morgan Jackson argues that the party’s recent success in the 2026 midterms resulted from focusing on economic issues and local concerns rather than national branding.
articles.body:
In the aftermath of 2024, experts were arguing not about whether Democrats could retake the U.S. Senate in 2026, but if we ever could. Forecasters projected Republicans holding at least 53 seats in the midterms, including North Carolina.

But because of candidates laser-focused on lowering costs for families in their state, as well as Republicans’ massive failure to tackle high prices and the corruption in Washington, we made history.

In North Carolina, Sen.-elect Roy Cooper (D) not only flipped a state President Trump carried all three times, but he did it by competing in suburban, exurban and rural areas — winning 21 counties Trump carried in 2024. By expanding the map and fighting to earn every vote, Cooper provided coattails that flipped an incredible six congressional seats , the state House and broke the state Senate supermajority. These historic victories, in potentially ten states that Trump carried, are worth celebrating. But we can’t take our foot off the gas, and we can’t fall into the same traps that previous midterm winners have fallen into. Democrats also need to take a clear look at ourselves.

Democrats may have carried the night on Tuesday, but 57 percent of Americans still have an unfavorable opinion of our party. As much as there is to celebrate, we should be clear-eyed that Tuesday was more about Republicans losing than it was about the national Democratic brand carrying us to victory. If we look at how Cooper or Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton (D-Kan.) won, it was by talking about diesel, not about being a Democrat.

Working families are sick of the chaos and corruption that has crushed their budgets and left them struggling to afford the basics. On Tuesday they gave Democrats a chance. Now, we need to deliver.

Cooper ran on a simple, catchy slogan: Make stuff cost less. He did not get distracted by shiny objects or hot-button issues that the D.C. political class was spinning themselves up about day after day. He talked about what voters were experiencing every single day: high prices. His message resonated not because it drove clicks or viral moments but because it was rooted in making daily life for everyday people easier.

Cooper vowed to not become a lobbyist and refused to own or trade individual stocks, so that North Carolinians knew that he would focus on their wallet, not his own. If we fail to deliver for these folks, 2028 will be the same as 2026, 2024 and 2020 — an election where voters hit the change button yet again.

Instead of ceding ground on crime as far too many folks in our party do, Cooper proudly ran on his record keeping families safe by putting violent criminals behind bars, going after drug dealers, opposing defunding the police and strengthening bail laws as attorney general and governor.

This is the path Democrats must take in order to win in 2028 and bring the American Dream back within reach for so many families: talk like normal people and work to make groceries cheaper.

Delivering results for families doesn’t mean we roll over to this administration. Because of how Trump has weaponized tariffs to reward his cronies, families are paying more at the grocery store. Because of how this administration has started a reckless war, families have paid record fuel prices for months and Americans have been killed .

Accountability is important, not for the sake of getting even, but for the sake of delivering a better life for working people. But if we take our eye off the main goal of lowering costs, if we become more preoccupied with evening the score then lowering the grocery bill, we won’t have done any good for families who entrusted us with their vote and are still struggling to get by.

Voters spoke loud and clear on Tuesday. We have some power, again. And with that power comes responsibility. But we cannot confuse us winning with them losing. If we want to win in the future, if we want to win in 2028, we can’t let this opportunity go to waste: we have to focus on the issues that matter and deliver a more affordable future for families across this country.

Morgan Jackson was a general consultant on Roy Cooper’s campaign and senior advisor to Cooper.

articles.title: Man accused in WHCA dinner shooting faces new terrorism charge
articles.summary: Cole Tomas Allen, the man accused of attempting to assassinate President Trump at the White House Correspondents’ Association (WHCA) dinner earlier this year, faces an additional charge of terrorism , new court filings showed Thursday. Allen allegedly ran past security, shot a Secret Service agent and attempted to enter the ballroom to shoot the president…
articles.body:
Cole Tomas Allen, the man accused of attempting to assassinate President Trump at the White House Correspondents’ Association (WHCA) dinner earlier this year, faces an additional charge of terrorism , new court filings showed Thursday.

Allen allegedly ran past security , shot a Secret Service agent and attempted to enter the ballroom to shoot the president at the annual dinner in April. He originally pleaded not guilty to attempted murder of the president, assaulting an officer of the United States and two federal gun charges.

The U.S. attorney’s office for the District of Columbia brought the additional charge of committing an act of terrorism while armed, claiming Allen attempted to kill Trump with the intent of influencing executive branch policy and intimidating a “significant portion of the civilian population.”

A California native, Allen is said to have written a manifesto prior to the assassination attempt that made clear he wished to target members of the Trump administration. His family was made aware of Allen’s plans minutes before the incident and alerted the local police, according to NBC News .

Jeanine Pirro, U.S. attorney for D.C., was in attendance at the dinner and is overseeing the prosecution of the case. Allen moved to disqualify Pirro, as she is an alleged victim of the crime he is accused of committing, but he was unsuccessful .

Allen is the latest of three gunmen charged with attempting to assassinate Trump. The first was at a 2024 rally in Butler, Pa., while the second was at a Florida golf course months later. The third, Allen, was at the annual dinner earlier this year.

articles.title: Trump ‘gaslighting’ over Huang controversy: Kara Swisher
articles.summary: Left-leaning journalist Kara Swisher criticized President Trump’s response to former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s scandal involving an extramarital affair with a suspected Chinese spy, saying the president is downplaying the seriousness of the allegations. “He has to say nothing’s going on here … because if there were, he’s in real trouble,” Swisher told CNN’s Kaitlan…
articles.body:
Left-leaning journalist Kara Swisher criticized President Trump’s response to former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s scandal involving an extramarital affair with a suspected Chinese spy, saying the president is downplaying the seriousness of the allegations.

“He has to say nothing’s going on here … because if there were, he’s in real trouble,” Swisher told CNN’s Kaitlan Collins in a Thursday interview. “This is serious national security issues, and to pretend that it’s not a big deal is kind of ridiculous. It’s gaslighting, you know, which is what he does all the time whenever something happens.”

Huang resigned as CEO of the chipmaker and tech giant Thursday after reports that he had multiple extramarital affairs, including with a woman named Alice Huang, whom the U.S. government suspected of being a spy for the Chinese government.

Trump has mostly stood by Jensen Huang , calling him an “honorable man” and saying the situation was “sad,” though he said in an interview Thursday that if the woman is indeed a spy for China, then Jensen Huang was right to resign.

The New York Times reported Thursday that Trump called Huang and told him to fight for his job.

The Times previously reported that Trump was told twice about Huang’s relationship with the woman and her suspected connections to China but did not appear to do anything with the information. Two months after the first time he was notified, he reversed course and allowed Nvidia to sell its highly advanced chips to China.

Now, members of both parties are calling for an investigation .

Multiple House Republicans have said they want Jensen Huang to brief them behind closed doors on his relationship with the woman and potential security concerns, while some Democrats want to look into what Trump knew and what he did about it.

Sens. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) and Jim Banks (R-Ind.) have called on Congress to pass their bill restricting Chinese access to advanced chips like Nvidia’s.

Swisher told Collins that there needed to be an investigation in Congress and that she did not trust the administration to look into the matter given Trump’s involvement.

Trump is “trying to throw doubt in a situation that requires real investigative work, which I don’t expect from either Todd Blanche or Kash Patel,” Swisher said, referring to the attorney general and FBI director, respectively. “It’s up to Congress to really look at this. And it looks like the Republican senators are at least taking national security issues seriously.”

Even if Republicans do not agree to look into it in the next few weeks, Democrats’ big midterm wins put them in comfortable majorities in both chambers starting in January, when they will control investigations and have subpoena power.

The incoming chair of the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), has already said he wants to pursue investigations of Trump and his allies. The White House vowed to respond aggressively .

articles.body:
Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) announced Thursday night he will challenge Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) to become the majority leader of the upper chamber next Congress, as Schumer faces dissent from new senators in particular.

“I think that we heard loud and clear from the American people that they want to end the war in Iran and bring down prices,” Van Hollen told MS NOW’s Jen Psaki. “We should do it now. We shouldn’t say we’re going to wait till January.”

As of Friday, he appears to have support from Sens. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.), Sens.-elect Peggy Flanagan (Minn.), Adam Hamilton (D-Kan.), Annie Andrews (D-S.C.), Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.) and Troy Jackson (D-Maine).

Sanders and Slotkin appeared together at a news conference on Tuesday and said they would not back Schumer. Some incoming senators said the same , including Sens.-elect Adam Hamilton (D-Kan.), Annie Andrews (D-S.C.), Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.) and Troy Jackson (D-Maine).

Microsoft’s catastrophic Outlook outage started easing on Friday morning, more than 18 hours after it turned off email for millions of people.

Alito implored Congress to fund the high court and chastised lower judges for sometimes issuing “unjustified” orders blocking presidents’ policies.
